messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 54, Daniel had spent most of his adult life working as a forester, and before the accident he thought of himself as a steady man in rough country, someone who could read terrain, judge risk, and keep other people safe in it. The event that broke that certainty happened on a logging access road during a routine day in the field. He had been guiding a younger crew member through a section where heavy timber had recently shifted. In a moment he still replays with sickening precision, Daniel made a call about where the man should stand while they moved around a hung-up trunk. The movement was not what Daniel expected. The log rolled and pinned the other man hard enough to cause catastrophic injuries without killing him. Daniel remembers the sound first, then the posture he was forced into as he dropped beside him, twisted at the waist and down on one knee, trying to hold weight off the man’s body while shouting for help. He can still see the injured worker’s face turned up toward him at close range, shocked and pleading, and it is that nearness that now makes other people’s physical presence feel loaded and dangerous rather than ordinary.

In the weeks afterward, reminders did not stay in the past. If his hip or lower back flared after a day outdoors, the physical pain pulled him straight back to the position he had been in on the road; he would stiffen and feel, for a few moments, as if his body were again braced over the trapped man. Seeing the injured worker at a follow-up meeting, or even catching sight of someone who resembled him, brought back not only the image but a wave of grief so strong Daniel had to look away. At other times the memory came with a burst of rage that startled him—rage at the accident, at the scene, at himself for having made the judgment he made. Each return of the memory seemed to confirm something he had come to believe: that there was something flawed in him that had made this happen, that his own judgment could not be trusted, and that the work that once defined him was no longer something he was truly capable of doing.

Those beliefs began to shape the way he moved through his days. On job sites he found himself watching everyone closely, scanning for where others were standing and how near they were to him, as if any ordinary approach might suddenly turn into another irreversible mistake. When a stranger came up behind him at a gas station or stepped toward him on a trailhead, his body reacted before his mind could catch up; he felt threatened and tightened through his shoulders, unable to relax even when he knew, logically, that he was safe. That state of constant watchfulness made him more likely to notice bodies nearby, faces, small movements, the very kinds of cues that set off the memory of the injured man. The more he monitored the people around him, the more often he stumbled into reminders of the accident.

At work this had become especially clear. Forestry had always meant close physical coordination with other men in unpredictable spaces, but now proximity itself was hard for Daniel to bear. If a coworker leaned in beside him to inspect a map or stepped too close while discussing a stand boundary, Daniel’s mind jumped to the pinned worker’s face and to his own body crouched in that impossible position. The memory was not just visual; he felt himself bodily reenacting it, bracing and twisting as if the weight were again in his hands. After episodes like that he became even less able to settle, and his inability to relax sharpened his sense that anyone nearby might be a source of danger. He had started taking the edge of a group, hanging back from crew conversations, and choosing tasks that let him stay physically apart, which his coworkers noticed as irritability and distance.

Over months, the threat never stayed confined to the moment. Being on guard around strangers, or around crew members moving unpredictably near him, fed the memories; then the memories fed his conviction that he was no longer the man he had been. If he could freeze inside his own body at a reminder, if grief and rage could overtake him in the middle of a workday, then to Daniel this meant he could not rely on himself. When pain in his body triggered the scene again, he took it as proof that the accident had marked him at the deepest level. Even seeing the injured man’s name in a message from the company could undo him for the rest of the day and leave him thinking that some essential defect in him had been exposed.

His marriage has narrowed around this. His wife says he is present but never at ease, always tracking sounds outside or the movement of people in a restaurant, and he has stopped joining friends for community events because the closeness of others makes him feel trapped and on alert. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent field inspection in which a younger worker approached from behind to ask a routine question, and Daniel spun, heart pounding, already half in the accident before he recognized where he was. Later that evening his back ached, and with the pain came the full bodily memory, the grief, and the familiar certainty that he had no business leading anyone. He came in frightened that this is permanent—that he has become dangerous through his own unreliability—but also hoping, cautiously, that he might find some way to be near other people again without feeling that another life could be ruined by his next mistake.
